item.title: Priyank Kharge targets Mangaluru with Rs 6,000 Cr regional growth push
item.description: Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge is urging investment in Mangaluru, with Dakshina Kannada contributing 5.3% of the state’s GDP. The Beyond Bengaluru strategy aims to unlock the region’s business and talent potential.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru may be Karnataka’s best-known technology hub, but the state government wants companies to look further along the coast. Mangaluru, with its established educational institutions, skilled workforce and quality of life, is being positioned as another centre for economic growth.

At the inauguration of Deloitte’s 27th office in India, in Mangaluru, Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge called on industry leaders to invest in the region and help create opportunities closer to where talent already lives.

Kharge said Dakshina Kannada is Karnataka’s second-largest district contributor to the state’s GDP after Bengaluru, accounting for 5.3% of the total. He said the region’s economic strength and talent pool make it an important part of the state’s next phase of growth.

“Our objective through Beyond Bengaluru is to take opportunities to where talent already exists, rather than expecting talent to move to Bengaluru,” he said.

He also acknowledged Deloitte’s decision to establish an office in Mangaluru, thanking Romal Shetty and the company’s team for supporting the government’s regional development agenda.

Building growth beyond Bengaluru

The government’s Beyond Bengaluru strategy aims to develop multiple economic centres by building on the strengths of different regions.

Kharge pointed to a recent Karnataka Cabinet meeting held in Mangaluru for the first time in the city’s history. The meeting identified growth opportunities for the region, with approximately Rs 6,000 crore committed towards its development.

He also cited the Local Economy Acceleration Programme (LEAP), which focuses on identifying regional strengths, attracting investment and creating employment.

Mangaluru, he said, has an agile talent pool and some of the country’s leading educational institutions. Its quality of life could also help companies attract and retain employees.

As an example, he mentioned a Danish team from software firm EG that surfs at Sasihithlu beach in the morning before heading to work. Kharge said such advantages could help the city stand out as a business destination.

Developing more employment centres across Karnataka could also ease pressure on Bengaluru, which continues to attract migrants from across the country.

Connecting education with industry

Attracting companies is only one part of the plan. Priyank Kharge said industry and educational institutions must work together to ensure graduates have the skills required by employers.

He called on companies such as Deloitte to help shape curricula and prepare students for emerging job opportunities.

“Why should a student studying in Mangaluru not be equipped to work with a company like Deloitte?” he asked, describing this as an opportunity for industry and government to work together.

The Minister also suggested exploring a Centre of Excellence in Mangaluru, potentially focused on health sciences, given the region’s established healthcare ecosystem.

Startups and new opportunities

Priyank Kharge encouraged entrepreneurs from the region to apply to the state’s ELEVATE programme, which offers eligible startups equity-free grants of up to Rs 1 crore.

He also outlined Karnataka’s regulatory sandbox initiative, which allows startups working on public-sector challenges, including urban mobility, to test their solutions with the government. Successful pilots can then be scaled across the state and potentially taken to other states.

The programme has enrolled 16 startups so far, with the government aiming to increase participation to 100.

The government’s message to businesses was that Karnataka’s next phase of growth need not be concentrated in Bengaluru. By bringing investment, skills development and startup opportunities to cities such as Mangaluru, it hopes to build more regional economic centres across the state.

item.title: Wiz webinar: Bringing a sharper, connected focus to AI security
item.description: From AI discovery to threat detection, Wiz brings security into focus in a new virtual webinar
item.content:encoded:
AI applications are becoming an increasingly important part of cloud environments. As adoption increases, so does the attack surface - far beyond traditional cloud assets. Today, organisations are building and deploying more AI-powered applications, agents, integrations and third-party tools. This leaves their security teams with a new challenge on their hands: understanding not just what exists, but what these applications can access and how their risks connect.

An AI application could interact with cloud systems, Application Programming Interfaces (API), sensitive data and other tools. Agents can retrieve information, call tools and trigger workflows. For security teams, looking at these assets individually may not reveal how their permissions, infrastructure and data access could interact to create security risk.

What to expect

To explore how organisations can address these challenges, global cybersecurity organization Wiz is hosting a focused 60-minute technical demo called ‘Securing Modern AI Applications with Wiz, featuring Dharmesh Vaya, Sr. Solution Engineer, Wiz.

The session will demonstrate how Wiz brings together an understanding of AI applications and cloud security context to secure AI from code to runtime, wherever it is built and run.

Event details

  • Date: December 11, 2026
  • Time: 03:00 PM
  • Format: Virtual event
  • Speaker: Dharmesh Vaya, Sr. Solution Engineer, Wiz

Understand what applications can do

Discovering an AI asset is just the first step. Security teams also need to understand what an application is designed to do, the tools it leverages, its capabilities, and access to data. During the demo, participants can discover how the Wiz AI Security Agent provides visibility into AI assets and custom applications, with deeper insights into agents, tools, and their capabilities. This feature examines agents and applications across code repositories, PaaS platforms, and self-hosted infrastructure like VMs, containers and serverless environments.

Connecting risks to identify critical attack paths

AI-related security risks do not exist in a silo. A vulnerability or misconfiguration can become more significant when connected to exposed infrastructure, privileged identities, or sensitive data.

The demo will showcase how the Wiz Security Graph connects AI-specific risks with exposure, identities, infrastructure, and sensitive data to uncover critical attack paths. Rather than flagging and treating security findings individually, this approach helps teams understand how different risks and vulnerabilities are intertwined. The Graph prioritises those with greater potential. For organisations working with multiple AI applications, agents, and integrations, this context can help security teams identify which connections need attention.

Securing AI: from code to runtime

As AI applications move from development into production, their behaviour, permissions, and exposure can change. Security, therefore, needs to extend across the application lifecycle. The session will demonstrate how Wiz brings together AI discovery, risk reduction, and runtime threat detection through one unified platform.

By connecting visibility into AI applications with contextual risk prioritisation and runtime threat detection, the platform aims to give security teams a more complete view of their AI-related exposure.

For organisations expanding their use of AI across cloud environments, understanding how applications, agents, identities, tools, and data interact is an important part of managing security risks.

Join for this 1-hour technical demo to see how Wiz connects these elements and helps teams secure AI applications from code to runtime.

Register now and learn how Wiz uncovers, connects, and secures AI risks.

item.title: Beyond UPI: Why many Indians still need help accessing basic banking services
item.description: Assisted banking is not an alternative to regular banks or the mobile application that banks provide. Through the extension of their services via designated local access points, banks can make use of the business correspondent model to extend basic banking functions to the local population.
item.content:encoded:
The digital payments revolution has changed the way transactions happen in India. In both urban and rural settings, transactions take place through the use of QR codes. The use of payment systems like UPI is common. According to the report by National Payments Corporation of India, as of October 2026, there were 25.47 billion transactions worth more than Rs 31.53 lakh crore made using UPI.

While there has been a quick shift towards the use of digital payments, the use of digital payments does not imply the use of routine banking services. Digital payments are only one component of routine banking services. Routine banking services include withdrawing cash, transferring money, and checking the balance. There has been uneven access to basic banking services in India despite the quick expansion in payment transactions.

Financial inclusion beyond opening bank accounts

Opening an account is the initial step of financial inclusion. According to the official PMJDY dashboard, the Department of Financial Services, under the Ministry of Finance of India, the total number of beneficiaries under Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was 59.63 crore as on 21 October 2026. 

The performance report demonstrates vast structural coverage: 46.29 crore beneficiaries come from rural and semi-urban areas, 33.26 crore beneficiaries are female beneficiaries, and deposits in accounts is Rs 3.25 lakh crore.

Having an account does not necessarily guarantee smooth operation through that account. An account itself does not make the trick when operational issues appear.

  • Distance problem: The process of getting to formal banking facilities costs time and daily wage.
  • Digital constraints: Many people have one smartphone in the family or do not know how to use complicated digital banking applications.
  • Operational issues: Issues such as language barrier in banking application, poor network connection, and possibility of transaction failures discourage usage of banking application independently.

It is crucial to note that digital literacy significantly varies depending on region, generation and social class. For some families, which rely on cash money, the possibility of taking out the money is as important as receiving anything

Why assisted banking continues to matter

Although self-service mobile applications eliminate all hassles for many individuals, there are many instances in which customers require personal help. In such a scenario, the banking correspondent (BC) model and assisted banking become invaluable.

Assisted banking is not an alternative to regular banks or the mobile application that banks provide. Through the extension of their services via designated local access points, banks can make use of the BC model to extend basic banking functions to the local population.

Local retailers authorised by the appropriate authorities act as an important connection in this case. Due to the regular visits made by community members to these retail outlets for daily necessities, the provision of secure technology in them will enable customers to access banking facilities without making an extra effort to visit a faraway branch of the bank.

This human-based service point acts as a reassuring factor for new users. Assistance from a trusted local retailer in withdrawing money, checking balance, or transferring money within the country will provide comfort to all types of users.

Digital literacy, security, and building trust

It is not enough just to increase access; making sure that usage is safe is equally important. The customer may be quite happy to effect a merchant payment via UPI but may be unsure as to how to authenticate the receipt and deal with any surprise payment failure.

Long-term confidence-building can be accomplished through a concentrated effort in three main directions:

  • Local language campaigns can educate customers on the issues of transaction authentication, fraud prevention, and safe use of the digital interface.
  • Intermediate accountability can ensure that all local service centres and BCs do their job with maximum transparency. Although customers enter their authentication details into the secure terminal by themselves, they should be constantly reminded never to share these details with anybody, including the intermediaries.
  • Grievance redressal is essential for cases of transaction failure to ensure that there is always a way out when something goes wrong, and if the customer’s money has been withdrawn from his or her account without completing the transaction.

The next phase must focus on usability

India has been rather successful in integrating millions of people into the formal financial sector with the help of various financial inclusion schemes. But, in the coming years, the attention must be on usability rather than integration of citizens in the formal financial sector.

It would take a joint effort from all the stakeholders in the ecosystem. On one hand, the banks have to ensure adequate availability and liquidity support to the local access points while, on the other hand, the technology companies have to develop an intuitive system that accommodates different levels of digital literacy.

In short, financial inclusion does not necessarily entail moving everything on a smartphone.

The author is Founder and CEO of Ezeepay, a digital financial services platform.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: 7 Underrated non-fiction books worth adding to your reading list
item.description: Discover seven underrated non-fiction books on psychology, creativity, personal growth and human behaviour that deserve a place on your reading list.
item.content:encoded:
Non-fiction books have a unique way of changing how we understand the world, ourselves and the people around us. While popular titles often dominate reading recommendations, some equally fascinating books receive far less attention than they deserve.

From understanding human happiness and exploring the psychology of everyday decisions to discovering the stories behind historical events, non-fiction offers something for every curious reader.

If you are looking for something beyond the usual bestselling recommendations, these seven underrated non-fiction books deserve a place on your reading list.

7 Underrated non-fiction books worth adding to your reading list

1. The Art of Travel by Alain de Botton

What makes travelling meaningful? Is it visiting famous landmarks, exploring unfamiliar cities or simply experiencing something different from everyday life?

In The Art of Travel, Alain de Botton explores these questions through philosophy, personal experiences and observations of different destinations. Rather than presenting a conventional travel guide, he examines why people travel and how their expectations influence their experiences.

The book explores themes such as anticipation, beauty, curiosity and the relationship between travel and happiness. It also draws inspiration from artists, writers and thinkers, including Charles Baudelaire and Vincent van Gogh.

What makes it worth reading: It encourages readers to look beyond destinations and appreciate the small details, experiences and perspectives that make travelling meaningful.

2. The Geography of Bliss by Eric Weiner

In The Geography of Bliss, journalist Eric Weiner travels across different countries to investigate an interesting question: what makes people happy?

From Switzerland and Iceland to India and Qatar, he explores how culture, lifestyle, social connections and personal beliefs influence people's understanding of happiness.

Combining travel writing, research and humour, Weiner examines why some societies appear happier than others and whether happiness can be understood through geography.

The book also challenges the idea that happiness comes from the same things for everyone. What creates a satisfying life in one culture may look completely different in another.

What makes it worth reading: It offers an entertaining introduction to the psychology and cultural influences of happiness while encouraging readers to reconsider their own definition of a fulfilling life.

3. The Book of Delights by Ross Gay

In The Book of Delights, poet and essayist Ross Gay explores the importance of noticing small moments of happiness in everyday life.

The book is a collection of short essays written over a year, with each piece focusing on an experience, observation or interaction that brings him joy. These moments range from unexpected conversations and acts of kindness to encounters with nature and ordinary pleasures.

What makes the collection interesting is that Gay does not ignore the difficult realities of life. Instead, he explores how moments of delight can exist alongside grief, uncertainty and social challenges.

His writing encourages readers to become more attentive to their surroundings and recognise experiences they might otherwise overlook.

What makes it worth reading: It is a thoughtful reminder that happiness does not always come from major achievements. Sometimes, it can be found in the smallest parts of an ordinary day.

4. The Library Book by Susan Orlean

For anyone who loves books, libraries and the stories behind them, The Library Book offers a fascinating reading experience.

Susan Orlean investigates the 1986 fire at the Central Library of the Los Angeles Public Library, which destroyed or damaged hundreds of thousands of books. The incident remains one of the most significant library fires in American history.

While exploring the mystery surrounding the fire, Orlean also examines the history of public libraries, their cultural importance and the people who dedicate their lives to preserving knowledge.

The book moves between historical investigation, personal storytelling and reflections on how libraries bring communities together.

What makes it worth reading: It offers a fresh perspective on libraries, showing that they are much more than buildings filled with books. They are spaces that preserve memories, encourage learning and make knowledge accessible.

5. The Undoing Project by Michael Lewis

Why do intelligent people sometimes make irrational decisions? And why do two individuals looking at the same situation often reach completely different conclusions?

In The Undoing Project, Michael Lewis explores the work and friendship of psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose research transformed the understanding of human judgement and decision-making.

Through their experiments, the two researchers challenged the assumption that people always make rational choices. Their work revealed how cognitive biases, mental shortcuts and emotions influence everyday decisions.

Lewis presents their scientific discoveries through a narrative that also explores their personal relationship and intellectual partnership.

What makes it worth reading: It helps readers understand why human judgement is often imperfect and how unconscious biases can influence decisions in everyday life.

Also Read
7 Books that change how you view time and your future

6. The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks by Rebecca Skloot

The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks tells the extraordinary story of Henrietta Lacks, an African-American woman whose cancer cells were collected without her knowledge in 1951.

These cells, later known as HeLa cells, became one of the most important tools in medical research. They contributed to numerous scientific developments, including research related to vaccines, cancer and genetics. However, behind these scientific achievements was a family that remained largely unaware of how Henrietta's cells were being used.

Rebecca Skloot combines investigative journalism, medical history and the experiences of the Lacks family to explore questions of medical ethics, consent, race and scientific progress.

What makes it worth reading: It reveals the human story behind a major scientific breakthrough and encourages readers to think about the ethical responsibilities that come with medical research.

7. The Comfort Book by Matt Haig

In The Comfort Book, author Matt Haig brings together short reflections, observations, quotations and personal thoughts about finding hope during difficult moments.

Rather than following a traditional self-help structure, the book offers small pieces of encouragement that readers can return to whenever they need reassurance or perspective.

It explores themes such as uncertainty, loneliness, gratitude, resilience and the importance of appreciating everyday life.

Its short entries make it easy to read a few pages at a time without following a particular order. The book also reminds readers that difficult periods do not define their entire lives.

What makes it worth reading: It is a gentle companion for readers who prefer reflective writing and simple reminders about hope, patience and the value of ordinary experiences.

Final thoughts

The best non-fiction books do more than provide information. They introduce new perspectives, challenge familiar assumptions and encourage readers to become more curious about the world.

Whether you want to understand human behaviour through The Undoing Project, explore happiness through The Geography of Bliss or rediscover the beauty of everyday experiences through The Book of Delights, these books offer something different from conventional self-help and motivational reading.

You do not always need to follow bestseller lists to find your next favourite book. Sometimes, the most rewarding reading experiences come from discovering a title you had never considered picking up.

item.title: From selling drones to intelligence: Where will the next wave of value come from?
item.description: As the drone industry evolves, the focus is shifting from aircraft specifications to the value delivered to customers. The next phase of growth will be shaped by AI, software, integrated technologies and service-led business models.
item.content:encoded:
When we look at the value of a drone, it is easy to focus on the aircraft itself. How long can it fly? How much weight can it carry? How far can it travel? These are important questions, and they will continue to matter. But there is another question that deserves equal attention: what does the customer actually get from that flight?

A drone may spend several hours monitoring an area and return with a large volume of footage. Yet, if the operator has to spend several more hours reviewing that footage to identify something important, much of the benefit is lost. The real value lies not simply in collecting information, but in making sense of it and using it at the right time.

I believe this is where the next phase of the drone industry will take shape.

The value does not end when the drone lands

As drones become more widely used across defence, infrastructure, mapping, and homeland security, customer expectations are changing. Buying a drone is increasingly becoming the beginning of a larger operational requirement.

Consider a team monitoring a long stretch of border or inspecting a large infrastructure project. The drone can capture images, video and location data, but the customer needs more than these individual inputs. They need to know what has changed, whether something requires attention and what action should follow.

This is where software and artificial intelligence (AI) have a pivotal role to play. Automated video summaries, event detection, and searchable annotations can make it easier to find relevant information without having to watch hours of recordings. The idea is not to remove people from the decision-making process but to help them focus on what matters and make better-informed decisions.

Experience is difficult to replicate

There is something about technology that becomes clear only when it is used regularly in the field. A drone may perform well during testing, but actual operating conditions can be very different. Terrain, weather, temperature and connectivity can all affect how a system performs.

This is why the experience gained from real deployments matters. Across the industry, drone manufacturers are learning that building a reliable product is not just about getting the engineering right. It is also about understanding how customers use the technology, what difficulties they encounter and where improvements are needed.

The scale of deployments is important in this regard. Every mission provides an opportunity to understand how the aircraft, payload, software and communication systems perform in real conditions. Repeated operations can also reveal patterns that may not emerge during controlled testing.

Over time, this learning becomes an advantage. Companies that stay closely connected to actual operating conditions are better placed to develop technology that works outside controlled testing environments. It also helps them understand what customers need, rather than relying only on what they initially ask for.

Technology must work together

Intelligence is not limited to what happens to the data after a flight. It also depends on whether the drone can complete its mission reliably in the first place.

For instance, a drone operating in a challenging environment needs dependable communication and navigation. In defence applications, electronic interference, jamming and spoofing can create additional complications. Similarly, operations in remote locations may have limited network connectivity, making it important to process certain information closer to where it is collected.

This is why the industry needs to look at the entire technology stack rather than treating the aircraft, software, payload and communication systems as separate elements. Secure command-and-control systems, resilient navigation, edge computing and specialised payloads all contribute to the final outcome.

This shift is also reflected in India's evolving defence procurement priorities. The Defence Acquisition Council's recent approval of capital acquisition proposals worth approximately Rs 2.12 lakh crore includes requirements for Long Range UAS, Surveillance UAV, Integrated Surveillance and Strike Systems, and Long Range Kamikaze Drone Systems. With approximately 82% of the proposed procurements earmarked for the Indian industry, the direction is significant. It signals an opportunity for domestic manufacturers to move beyond building individual platforms towards developing integrated, mission-ready capabilities that address increasingly complex operational requirements.

This also helps reduce dependence on external technologies in areas where control, security and reliability are particularly important.

The business model will evolve with the technology

This shift also has implications for how drone companies build sustainable businesses. Hardware sales will remain an important part of the industry. However, the opportunity extends well beyond the initial sale of an aircraft. A drone has an operating lifecycle that involves software, analytics, maintenance, upgrades, training and support. Each of these can contribute to the value delivered to a customer over time.

Models such as Drone-as-a-Service, software subscriptions and analytics-led solutions can allow customers to access drone capabilities without having to manage every aspect of ownership and operations themselves. For providers, these models can create opportunities for longer-term customer relationships and a more diversified revenue mix.

From a business perspective, this also creates opportunities for repeat engagements and more predictable customer relationships. But these models will succeed only when they offer a clear economic or operational benefit. A customer will continue paying for a service if it helps reduce manual effort, improve efficiency or deliver information that was previously difficult to access.

The objective should not simply be to introduce more software or services. It should be to make the overall solution more useful to the customer.

The next opportunity is in delivering outcomes

The drone industry is still evolving, and there are challenges to address, particularly around data security, system integration, reliability and the economics of scaling these solutions. Not every application will require the same level of automation or intelligence. What matters is understanding the customer's actual requirement and developing technology accordingly.

As the market matures, I expect customers to place greater emphasis on the outcome rather than the specifications of the aircraft alone. They will want to know whether a drone can help them monitor an area more effectively, complete an inspection faster or respond to an incident with better information.

The aircraft will remain at the centre of this ecosystem, but it will be one part of a much larger solution. The companies that understand this shift early and invest in the right capabilities will be better positioned for the industry's next phase of growth.

Ultimately, the future of drones will not be determined only by how far they can fly or how long they can stay in the air but it will depend on how effectively every flight can be translated into intelligence, action and measurable value for the customer.

(Vipul Joshi is the CFO at ideaForge, an Indian aerospace and defense company)

item.title: Why you must read Jordan Himelfarb’s New Chess book
item.description: Discover why Jordan Himelfarb's Interregnum is a compelling read about ambition, rivalry, young chess prodigies and the battle to become world champion.
item.content:encoded:
Chess is often seen as a game of strategy, patience and intellectual ability. But behind every major tournament lies a world of ambition, intense preparation, personal sacrifices and the pressure to perform.

For elite players, becoming world champion is not simply about winning matches; it is about securing a place in the history of the game.

Jordan Himelfarb's Interregnum: Inside the Grueling & Glamorous Battle to Become the Next King of Chess explores this fascinating world through the stories of grandmasters competing for one of the most prestigious titles in sport.

The book follows a defining moment in modern chess: Magnus Carlsen's decision not to defend his world championship title for a fifth time. His announcement created an opportunity for other leading players to pursue a dream that had long seemed difficult to achieve.

Combining sports journalism, character studies and behind-the-scenes storytelling, Interregnum offers a closer look at the people competing at the highest level of chess.

Here is why this book deserves a place on your reading list.

Jordan Himelfarb’s new chess book: What makes it worth reading?

1. It takes you inside the battle for the world chess championship

For years, Magnus Carlsen's dominance made the race for the world championship particularly challenging for other elite players. His decision not to defend his title changed the competitive landscape and opened the door for a new champion.

Interregnum explores what happened next, following the grandmasters who saw an opportunity to achieve their lifelong ambitions. Rather than simply documenting tournament results, Himelfarb examines the competitive environment surrounding the championship race. Readers get a sense of what it means to pursue a title that can define an entire career.

For anyone curious about professional chess, this offers an engaging perspective on the competition beyond the board.

2. It explores the personalities behind the chess pieces

One of the most interesting aspects of Interregnum is its focus on the individuals behind the game. Elite chess players are often recognised for their ratings, tournament victories and playing styles.

However, they also have personal ambitions, insecurities, unconventional personalities and different approaches to handling pressure. Himelfarb explores the lives and mindsets of these grandmasters, showing how their backgrounds and experiences influence their journeys.

The book also examines the contrast between established players whose opportunities may be running out and younger prodigies determined to make their mark.

This makes the story about much more than chess. It becomes a study of ambition, competition and human psychology.

3. It introduces readers to the changing world of chess

Chess has experienced a remarkable resurgence in recent years, attracting new audiences through online platforms, streaming and digital communities. Interregnum explores this changing landscape, including the influence of younger, internet-savvy players who are reshaping how the game is experienced and discussed.

The book captures the contrast between chess's centuries-old traditions and the modern personalities bringing fresh energy to the sport.

For readers who have followed the growing popularity of online chess, this offers an opportunity to understand the people and developments behind that transformation.

It also highlights how an ancient intellectual pursuit continues to find new audiences in a digitally connected world.

4. You don't need to be a chess expert to enjoy it

One reason people hesitate to pick up books about chess is the assumption that they need to understand complicated strategies, openings and technical terminology.

However, Interregnum is not designed as a traditional chess instruction manual. According to the book's description, it combines elements of a sports chronicle, character study and celebration of the game.

Its storytelling focuses on the personalities, ambitions and rivalries that make the championship race compelling.

The book also uses technical details without overwhelming readers with chess terminology. As highlighted in reviews by The New Yorker and Deccan Herald, its accessibility makes it appealing even to those unfamiliar with the finer details of competitive chess.

You can therefore enjoy the human stories and competitive drama without being an experienced player.

5. It shows the psychological side of competition

Competing at the highest level requires more than intelligence or technical preparation. Players must also manage expectations, anxiety, setbacks and the pressure of performing when the stakes are high.

Interregnum explores these emotional dimensions through the experiences of grandmasters pursuing the world championship.

The contrast between experienced competitors and young prodigies also raises interesting questions about timing, opportunity and ambition. Some players are racing against time, while others are only beginning their journeys.

These experiences make the book relatable beyond professional chess. Anyone pursuing a demanding personal or professional goal can recognise the tension between ambition, uncertainty and the desire to succeed.

About the Author: Jordan Himelfarb

Jordan Himelfarb is a managing editor at the Toronto Star, one of North America's major newspapers. He oversees coverage across politics, national and international affairs, and opinion.

Before becoming managing editor, he served as the newspaper's politics editor and deputy editorial page editor. He has also received three National Newspaper Award nominations, recognising his work in journalism and editing.

Interestingly, Himelfarb was previously a competitive Scrabble player before turning his attention to chess and contract bridge.

His experience in journalism and his interest in intellectually demanding games come together in Interregnum, which approaches chess through reporting, observation and character-driven storytelling.

Final thoughts

Interregnum: Inside the Grueling & Glamorous Battle to Become the Next King of Chess offers a different way to experience the world of competitive chess. Instead of focusing exclusively on moves, strategies and tournament outcomes, Jordan Himelfarb explores the people, personalities and ambitions shaping the modern game.

Whether you follow international chess, enjoy sports journalism or simply appreciate stories about individuals pursuing extraordinary goals, this book offers an engaging reading experience.

Its biggest appeal lies in showing that behind every intellectual battle is a human story filled with ambition, uncertainty, rivalry and the desire to leave a lasting legacy.

item.title: 5 Lessons from Traitor in the House by Shubha Menon
item.description: Explore five powerful lessons from Shubha Menon's Traitor in the House, a memoir about mental health, family trauma, caregiving and resilience.
item.content:encoded:
Traitor in the House: My Bipolar Life by Shubha Menon is a deeply personal memoir about growing up in a family affected by bipolar disorder. Through experiences of childhood trauma, caregiving, denial and eventual diagnosis, Menon explores how untreated mental illness can shape relationships and affect generations.

The book moves beyond the experiences of one individual to examine the emotional realities of families living with mental health challenges. It also explores how understanding, acceptance and self-awareness can help people confront painful experiences.

5 Meaningful lessons from Traitor in the House by Shubha Menon

1. Mental illness should be understood, not judged

One of the most important lessons from the memoir is that mental illness should never be treated as a personal failure or a character flaw. Through her mother's experiences with bipolar disorder, Menon shows how a lack of awareness and understanding can make an already difficult situation more painful for an entire family.

The book highlights the importance of recognising mental health conditions, seeking professional help and replacing judgement with compassion.

Lesson: Understanding someone's struggles is the first step towards treating them with empathy rather than blame.

2. Childhood experiences can shape adult life

The experiences we have during childhood can influence how we think, behave and build relationships as adults. Menon reflects on growing up in an unpredictable family environment and how those experiences affected her sense of safety and emotional well-being.

The memoir demonstrates that painful childhood memories do not simply disappear with age. They can influence how people respond to stress, relationships and difficult situations later in life.

Lesson: Acknowledging childhood trauma is important because healing often begins with understanding how the past has shaped the present.

3. Unaddressed trauma can pass through generations

The book explores how the effects of trauma can extend beyond one individual and influence future generations. Menon's family history reveals how unresolved emotional pain, untreated mental illness and unhealthy coping patterns can affect relationships between parents and children.

However, recognising these patterns creates an opportunity to approach them differently. Understanding family history can help individuals identify harmful behaviours and make conscious choices to avoid repeating them.

Lesson: You may not be responsible for the pain passed down through your family, but you can take steps to prevent harmful patterns from continuing.

4. Caregivers need emotional support too

Families supporting someone with a serious mental health condition often experience emotional exhaustion, fear and uncertainty. While their attention naturally focuses on the person who needs care, their own emotional well-being can easily be overlooked.

Menon's account highlights the complicated realities of growing up in a caregiving environment, where love, responsibility, fear and frustration can exist together.

It reminds readers that supporting someone through mental illness should not mean ignoring their own emotional needs.

Lesson: Caring for someone else should not require abandoning yourself. Caregivers also deserve understanding, support and space to heal.

5. Acceptance can become the beginning of healing

One of the most powerful aspects of Menon's journey is her gradual movement from fear and denial towards diagnosis, understanding and acceptance.

The memoir shows that confronting painful experiences is not easy, but acknowledging reality can make it possible to seek help and develop healthier ways of coping.

Acceptance does not mean approving of everything that happened or forgetting the past. It means recognising what happened without allowing it to define every part of your future.

Lesson: Healing begins when you stop running away from difficult truths and start understanding them with honesty and compassion.

5 Lessons about self-acceptance from Why Is My Skin Brown

Final thoughts

Traitor in the House: My Bipolar Life is more than a memoir about living with bipolar disorder. It is an exploration of family relationships, childhood experiences, generational trauma and the complicated journey towards understanding oneself.

Through her personal experiences, Shubha Menon encourages readers to look at mental illness with greater empathy and recognise the importance of addressing emotional wounds rather than keeping them hidden.

The book leaves readers with an important reminder: understanding the past does not change what happened, but it can help us make different choices about the future.

item.title: India, Australia deepen education ties with focus on skills and edtech
item.description: India and Australia are deepening education ties through partnerships in edtech, vocational training and higher education, with a growing emphasis on workforce development and future skills.
item.content:encoded:
Australia is expanding its education relationship with India into joint training, digital learning and workforce development, as a 21-member Australian delegation visits New Delhi and Bengaluru from November 23 to 27. 

Led by the Australian Trade and Investment Commission (Austrade), and supported by Investment NSW and Trade & Investment Queensland, the group is attending DIDAC India 2026 at Bengaluru’s Bangalore International Exhibition Centre from November 25 to 27. 

It includes universities, vocational providers and edtech firms working across schools, employability and workforce development.

Vik Singh, Austrade’s Trade and Investment Commissioner, said the delegation would connect education more closely with economic needs. 

“Through this delegation, we are placing skills development and EdTech at the centre of our collaboration, connecting institutions, industry, governments and learners to build the skills needed for future economic growth. This is about building meaningful partnerships that bring education, technology and workforce needs closer together,” Singh noted.

Eight Australian universities are operating or preparing to establish a presence in India. Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade lists five Australian university branch campuses opened since 2024, in Gujarat’s GIFT City, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Greater Noida. 

Education is Australia’s largest service export to India, valued at A$9.4 billion in 2025, when more than 140,000 Indian students were studying in Australia.

India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 prioritises access, equity, quality and internationalisation in higher education. University Grants Commission rules introduced in 2023 opened the way for eligible foreign universities to establish campuses. 

In December 2025, the bilateral Education and Skills Council backed online and blended learning, dual qualifications and employer-aligned courses, while citing the RMIT-BITS Pilani partnership and Monash University’s teacher-training initiative in Uttar Pradesh.

In July 2026, India’s National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) and Australia’s Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) signed a letter of intent on vocational-training quality assurance, with qualification benchmarking and possible recognition among areas for further exploration. 

The four-year Australia-India Future Skills Initiative supports partnerships for short courses and micro-credentials, short units that certify specific skills, in digital technology, energy, healthcare and infrastructure.

item.title: Karnataka names 47 startup winners under ELEVATE 2026
item.description: The list includes Agribotic Systems, Arthaveda, Arys Garage, Aviominds Global, Carnad Engineering, Ganesis Semiconductors, Gridflow Technologies, Insulin Yogi, Jatayu Saga, Pravaaha Biotech, Prakashikam Space, VIVIDSILICON, Wayve Electric, XALES AI, and others.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka has selected 47 startups under ELEVATE 2026, the general call within its flagship early-stage grant-in-aid programme. It is one of four calls in the 2026 edition.

Together, ELEVATE 2026, Aspire, Shakti and Unnati selected 196 startups. The programmes offer grants of up to Rs 50 lakh and aligns with the Karnataka Startup Policy 2025-2030 and the Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP).

ELEVATE 2026 has 47 winners, with a cut-off score of 70.00. Aspire selected 69, Shakti 63, and Unnati 17, including 14 SC-led and three ST-led ventures. The 47 selected startups are from the general ELEVATE call, not the separate ELEVATE NxT deep-tech programme.

The geographical distribution highlights Bengaluru's dominance: 42 winners are based in Bengaluru Urban and three in Bengaluru Rural. Dharwad and Gadag account for one winner each. This means 45 of the 47 selected startups are from the two Bengaluru districts, with only two from elsewhere in Karnataka.

The selected startups include Agribotic Systems, Arthaveda, Arys Garage, Aviominds Global, Carnad Engineering, Ganesis Semiconductors, Gridflow Technologies, Insulin Yogi, Jatayu Saga, Pravaaha Biotech, Prakashikam Space, VIVIDSILICON, Wayve Electric and XALES AI.

The selection process, conducted between July and October, involved four stages: data checks, pitch-deck reviews, multi-city pitching sessions and an in-person finale in Bengaluru. Across the four calls, the programme received 2,429 applications, of which 2,213 cleared the initial data-sufficiency check. Of the 627 finalists, 624 were evaluated, resulting in the selection of 196 startups across the four cohorts.

Launched in 2017, ELEVATE has supported more than 1,227 startups, with over Rs 280 crore in funding committed, according to the 2025 Bengaluru Innovation Report.

In September 2026, the Karnataka Cabinet approved three initiatives to strengthen the state's innovation ecosystem: a Rs 35 crore AI Hub at IIIT-Bengaluru, a Rs 42.83 crore drone-testing facility and a Rs 25 crore Government First initiative under ELEVATE to promote innovation-led public procurement.

item.title: Amazon’s cumulative ecommerce exports from India reach $27B
item.description: The milestone marks continued progress towards Amazon’s goal of enabling $80 billion in cumulative ecommerce exports from India by 2030, the company said.
item.content:encoded:
Ecommerce major Amazon on Wednesday said it has reached $27 billion in cumulative ecommerce exports from India through its Amazon Global Selling programme, with the number of exporters on the platform rising 20% in a year to 2.4 lakh.

The milestone marks continued progress towards Amazon’s goal of enabling $80 billion in cumulative ecommerce exports from India by 2030, the company said in a statement.

Launched in 2015, the programme has registered over 2.4 lakh exporters, who have sold more than one billion 'Made-in-India' products to customers across Amazon's global marketplaces.

The increase in cumulative exports was $7 billion this year, the same as last year, when it rose from $13 billion at the end of 2024 to $20 billion in October 2025.

"India has the potential to become a global powerhouse for consumer exports, and e-commerce is helping turn that ambition into reality, creating opportunities for every Indian seller to become a global exporter. We see tremendous opportunity in sectors like textiles, where India's manufacturing strengths, craftsmanship and entrepreneurial talent can translate into globally recognised brands," said Srinidhi Kalvapudi, Head of Amazon Global Selling in India.

He said the India-UK trade pact would benefit sellers as lower tariffs take effect, adding that it was still early days and a meaningful assessment would take about a year.

On the upcoming Budget 2027-28, Kalvapudi said the government has begun recognising e-commerce exports as a separate category requiring a different approach.

"We're hoping that they're going to double down on it in the coming budget," he said.

Delhi, with over 36,000 exporters, tops the list of states and Union Territories on the Amazon Global Selling programme, followed by Rajasthan (over 32,500), Uttar Pradesh (over 29,000), Gujarat (over 28,000) and Maharashtra (over 23,500), according to the company.

Among smaller cities, exporters from Erode in Tamil Nadu crossed $121.5 million in sales between January 2025 and the third quarter of 2026.

Health and personal care (45%), grocery (44%), beauty (42%) and toys (35%) emerged as the top-performing categories, recording the highest compound annual growth rates (CAGR) over the last 10 years, the company said.

The programme gives Indian sellers access to 18 or more Amazon stores in countries, including the US, UK, Germany, Canada, UAE, France, Italy and Spain.

item.title: PhonePe resumes IPO process; targets listing in Feb-March at $12-15B valuation
item.description: PhonePe had earlier deferred its public listing plans amid geopolitical uncertainties, weak macroeconomic conditions and heightened volatility in equity markets.
item.content:encoded:
PhonePe has revived its initial public offering (IPO) plans and is targeting a stock market listing in February-March at a valuation of $12-15 billion (around Rs 1.2 lakh crore to Rs 1.5 lakh crore), merchant bankers familiar with the development said.

The digital payments major is likely to file its revised draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) very soon. The proposed IPO is expected to raise Rs 12,000-14,000 crore and will entirely be an offer-for-sale (OFS), they added.

PhonePe had earlier deferred its public listing plans amid geopolitical uncertainties, weak macroeconomic conditions and heightened volatility in equity markets.

The company has now resumed preparations for the IPO, following an improvement in the broader market environment, stronger equity market sentiment and a recovery in its business performance, merchant bankers familiar with the development said.

The proposed listing is expected to be a significant milestone for India's digital payments and fintech sector.

The macroeconomic environment has improved, with foreign institutional investors (FPIs) returning to Indian equities. November has emerged as the strongest month so far in terms of FPI inflows.

The company's business performance has also gained momentum. After witnessing muted growth last year, PhonePe has returned to revenue growth of around 40% year-on-year, excluding merchant discount rate (MDR) and digital incentives, they said.

It has also turned profit-after-tax (PAT) positive at the group level in the first half of the current financial year, without adjusting for employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) costs. Its lending distribution business has nearly doubled year-on-year, they added.

item.title: Lakshmi Venu files suit seeking partition of Venu Srinivasan family assets
item.description: Lakshmi Venu has filed a suit in the Madras High Court seeking partition of Venu Srinivasan family assets and access to records, after efforts towards an amicable settlement failed to make progress.
item.content:encoded:
Lakshmi Venu, daughter of Venu Srinivasan, has filed a suit in the Madras High Court seeking partition of the joint-family assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family. 

A statement from Lakshmi Venu’s counsel said she seeks her claimed share and access to family records that she says have been withheld despite repeated requests.

The suit follows a November 16 partition notice to her father, who is Chairman Emeritus of TVS Motor and Non-Executive Chairman of TVS Holdings.

The statement said his reply did not recognise Lakshmi Venu's claim, and settlement efforts had failed. It noted the case concerns ownership, and not directed at the operations of any company, and that any partition should be given effect in an orderly manner.

Mallika Srinivasan supports her daughter. In a statement, she said, “It is unfortunate that the response to Lakshmi’s notice has not recognized her lawful rights and no progress has been made towards an amicable resolution. In these circumstances, she has been compelled to approach the Court to protect her rights.”

Queries have been sent to Venu Srinivasan seeking his response to Lakshmi Venu’s claims and the issues raised in the suit. This story will be updated if a response is received.

Lakshmi Venu’s statement dated November 16 identifies interests held through the VS Trust and other holding structures, including stakes in TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and TVS Holdings, formerly known as Sundaram-Clayton. She also alleges that the concentration of beneficial interest in favour of her brother Sudarshan Venu was to the exclusion of her own lawful rights.

The central question is whether the wider TVS family settlement of 2020 also settled the economic interests of the Venu Srinivasan branch.

A stock-exchange disclosure confirms that the four family members signed a further memorandum in March 2024, following the wider TVS family settlement based on a December 10, 2020 agreement, effective from February 4, 2022. It describes the 2024 memorandum as covering brand use and business restrictions, and says TVS Holdings was not a party and that its business was not adversely affected. The disclosure does not establish that the family assets were partitioned. 

Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan said no final economic settlement was reached. Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan, according to Financial Express, maintain that the arrangements were consensual, documented and binding.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Rodic Consultants proposes Rs 200 Cr fund for AI in infrastructure
item.description: The engineering consultancy will commit Rs 100 crore and expects to raise the rest from co-investors. Selected startups could test their products on live infrastructure projects.
item.content:encoded:
Infrastructure engineering consultancy Rodic Consultants on Wednesday announced plans to set up the Rs 200 crore Rodic AI Infrastructure Innovation Fund to back startups developing AI and other technologies for India’s infrastructure sector.

Rodic will commit Rs 100 crore to the proposed fund and expects to raise the remaining Rs 100 crore through co-investments from venture capital firms, angel funds and individual investors, including ultra-high-net-worth individuals. The company did not name any co-investors or disclose target cheque sizes.

Rodic said selected startups could test their products on live infrastructure projects, draw on its engineering expertise and explore partnerships with public and private sector organisations. The company has spent 26 years working on infrastructure projects across sectors including highways, bridges, tunnels, railways, metros, water and hydropower.

The company sees applications for these technologies across the life of a project, from planning and construction to monitoring and maintenance. Field trials would give startups a chance to see how their products perform on working sites and what needs to change before wider deployment.

“Innovators often need more than capital. They need access to real infrastructure problems, project sites, engineering expertise, data and potential users,” Raj Kumar, chairman and managing director of Rodic Consultants, said in a statement. He cited AI, computer vision, drones, sensors and robotics as technologies that could change how infrastructure is designed, built and maintained.

The announcement comes ahead of Rodic’s InfraAI Conclave on January 22, 2027, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. The company said the event would bring together government officials, infrastructure companies, investors, startups and researchers to discuss where AI can be used in the sector.

item.title: Piramal Alternatives invests Rs 225 Cr in Ardee Engineering
item.description: The investment will help Ardee expand manufacturing capacity and pursue larger industrial projects, including opportunities in data centres.
item.content:encoded:
Piramal Alternatives, the fund management arm of the Piramal Group, has announced an investment of Rs 225 crore in Ardee Engineering through Piramal India Credit Opportunities Fund II.

Ardee will use the capital to expand its manufacturing capacity and execute a growing pipeline of industrial projects.

The company designs and manufactures pre-engineered buildings and material handling systems for sectors such as manufacturing, warehousing and logistics. Its pre-engineered buildings business spans design, manufacturing and on-site installation management.

Ardee also supplies customised systems for moving and processing materials at industrial facilities. Its other engineering services include heavy structures, precision equipment and industrial automation.

Chairman and Managing Director Chandra Moturu said the capital would help Ardee pursue larger projects, including those in data centres. “The investment will provide us with additional resources to strengthen our capabilities, execute a growing pipeline of projects and pursue larger opportunities across our key sectors including emerging areas such as data centres,” he said.

For Piramal Alternatives, the deal is part of a strategy to provide flexible capital to established mid-market companies. The fund manager, which says it has $1.6 billion in assets under management, provides financing ranging from pure credit to structured investments.

Kalpesh Kikani, Managing Director and CEO of Piramal Alternatives, said rising investment in Indian manufacturing and industrial infrastructure was creating opportunities for engineering companies with a track record of executing complex projects.

Piramal Alternatives did not disclose the structure of the investment or provide a timeline for Ardee’s capacity expansion.

item.title: Goldman Sachs, Societe Generale buy Rs 920-Cr stake in Lenskart
item.description: The investors acquired a total of 1,26,97,702 equity shares on Monday, amounting to a 0.73% stake in Lenskart, as per the stock exchange data.
item.content:encoded:
Global financial giants Goldman Sachs and Societe Generale together bought nearly a 1% stake in eyewear retailer Lenskart Solutions for Rs 920 crore through separate block deals on the NSE.

The investors acquired a total of 1,26,97,702 equity shares on Monday, amounting to a 0.73% stake in Lenskart, as per the stock exchange data.

Goldman Sachs through its affiliates purchased 65.21 lakh shares in Gurugram-based Lenskart, while Societe Generale (SocGen) acquired 61.76 lakh shares of the company at an average price of Rs 725 apiece on the NSE.

The transactions amounted to a total value of Rs 920.58 crore.

On the selling side, San Francisco-based Steadview Capital Management offloaded an equal number of shares through its two affiliates at the same price on the National Stock Exchange (NSE).

Following the stake sale, global investment firm Steadview's holding in Lenskart has come down to 2.58% from 3.31%.

Shares of Lenskart fell nearly 4% to close at Rs 715.90 apiece on Monday.

Earlier this month, US-based Goldman Sachs and French financial services group Societe Generale were among the investors that acquired shares of Lenskart from Japanese technology investor SoftBank for Rs 1,896 crore.

item.title: VU Venture Partners launches India VC accelerator, investment platform
item.description: VU Venture Partners is bringing its venture-capital accelerator and startup investment platform to India, targeting early-stage companies while training prospective investors through Venture University.
item.content:encoded:
US-based VU Venture Partners is bringing its venture-capital investor accelerator to India and plans to evaluate investments of $100,000 to $1 million in local startups. It said it will focus on seed and Series A, early funding rounds for young companies, combining investor training with access to its global investment network.

The programme will be delivered through Venture University, which VU said it established in 2018. Its first Indian cohort is scheduled to begin on April 5, 2027, with up to 25 participants accepted each quarter. 

The 11-week course includes a 40-hour venture-capital masterclass and is followed by an apprenticeship of around three to 12 months alongside VU Venture Partners. Participants join one of nine sector teams, help assess investments and share in their cohort portfolio’s profits. VU said they may help select between seven and 28 investments over one to four cohorts.

The firm noted earlier cohorts collectively invested more than $80 million in over 125 companies, including SpaceX and OpenAI. 

Founder and General Partner J. Skyler Fernandes said the programme was intended to provide practical experience. “Venture University equips individuals with practical knowledge, skills and investment experience, helping them build a track record,” he said.

For startups, VU noted it will use its global fund and a syndicate of more than 8,000 accredited investors, a network that co-invests in individual deals, to assess Indian companies. Its stated interests include AI, robotics, space and defence, advanced computing, healthcare, fintech and industrials. 

The company said it has already invested in diagnostics and IVF provider Redcliffe Labs and hostel operator goSTOPS.

Anaina Malik, a partner on VU’s India team, said the firm wanted to connect founders with networks as well as capital. “India has a deep and diverse founder ecosystem, and we see an opportunity to connect ambitious Indian companies with the expertise and networks that can help them scale,” she said.

The launch comes as India’s private-capital market expands but becomes more selective. EY and the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association reported $60.7 billion in combined private-equity and venture-capital investment across 1,475 deals in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, investment totalled $17.1 billion, including $4.8 billion in startup deals.

Yet a Grant Thornton Bharat and IVCA report said domestic venture fundraising doubled to $5.4 billion in 2025 while seed funding fell 37% in the first nine months of 2026, pointing to tougher conditions for younger companies and emerging fund managers.

Other investors are also moving into specialist technology. Earlier this week, CortexSpark Ventures announced a Rs 1,000 crore deep-tech fund focused on areas including space, defence, robotics and AI.

Government schemes are intended to widen funding options. The Rs 10,000 crore Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 channels capital through registered alternative investment funds, pooled vehicles that invest in startups, rather than investing directly. 

The separate Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation scheme is designed to provide longer-term finance for areas including deep technology, AI, robotics and space.

item.title: Nexent Capital launches $1B fund focused on AI & data centres investments
item.description: The fund will deploy the capital in various modes such as private equity, credit and public equity.
item.content:encoded:
Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, a financial services firm, has launched Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting $1 billion in capital commitments for investments in quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy. The fund can be expanded up to a $1.6 billion hard cap.

According to a company statement, the fund is structured as an Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM)-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund (QIF), which will serve as the master fund. A GIFT City-based, IFSCA-regulated Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) will act as its feeder.

Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the fund's ADGM-based manager, with the company progressing towards authorisation from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA).

The statement said Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I will deploy capital across five areas: infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets; private credit and structured capital; special-situations M&A; growth equity and PIPEs; and liquid, public equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain.

The Fund has an anchor commitment of $20 million from the Tyagi family office and line of sight to an identified pipeline of quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy projects across North America and India, including data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform.

On the launch, Adesh Tyagi, Managing Partner, Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said, “AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure—power, land, and compute—that most capital isn’t positioned to finance at the scale or speed this moment demands. Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I is designed to meet that gap directly, giving institutional and family-office investors a disciplined way to back the infrastructure and energy assets that will underpin the next decade of AI growth.”

The statement said, the launch comes as global investors increasingly look to deploy capital into the physical infrastructure underpinning AI growth—power generation, data centers, and advanced energy systems — and as GIFT City and the Abu Dhabi Global Market continue to develop as complementary gateways for structuring cross-border alternative investment vehicles.

item.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to exit after over 11 years
item.description: Under Krishnamurthy’s leadership, Flipkart grew more than fivefold and strengthened its position in India’s ecommerce market. The company is now preparing for a leadership transition.
item.content:encoded:
Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy is set to step down after more than 11 years with the e-commerce company. His departure marks the end of a decade-long leadership stint during which the business grew more than fivefold.

The company announced on Wednesday that Krishnamurthy is concluding his tenure, adding that a successor will be announced in the coming weeks.

In the interim, Balaji Thiagarajan, currently Flipkart’s Chief Product and Technology Officer, and the company’s board will lead the organisation.

During Krishnamurthy’s leadership, Flipkart strengthened its position in India’s ecommerce market, expanded its reach across the country, and introduced several innovations for consumers and sellers. The company also established its Big Billion Days sale as a major fixture of India’s festive shopping season.

“It has been a privilege to be part of Flipkart’s journey. I am proud of the scale of the business we have built, but equally proud of how we have built it. Strong ethics, integrity and high standards of governance have been central to Flipkart’s growth,” said Krishnamurthy in a statement.

He added that the company had helped transform how millions of Indians shop while creating opportunities for sellers, entrepreneurs and businesses across the country.

Commenting on his departure, Chris Nicholas, President and CEO of Walmart International, said, “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled, and his many contributions to the company. We wish him nothing but the best as he moves on to his next adventure.”

Flipkart's parent Walmart reiterated its commitment to the ecommerce business and its long-term prospects in India. The company said Flipkart continues to have a strong market position and significant growth opportunities.

Established in 2007, Flipkart has expanded into a digital commerce group that includes Myntra, Flipkart Wholesale, Cleartrip, and super.money. The company said its platform has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including Shopsy sellers. Its marketplace offers more than 150 million products across over 80 categories.

Krishnamurthy’s departure comes as India's ecommerce market continues to evolve, with competition intensifying across online retail and quick commerce. Flipkart has been expanding its services and strengthening its position against rivals, including Amazon and emerging digital commerce platforms.

The company did not disclose Krishnamurthy’s next plans.

item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here’s the roundup for Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

A statement from the VC firm said, Aeravti Ventures II has secured commitments as the first close of its target corpus with the final close expected within the next six months.

Aeravti Ventures II plans to invest in 9–10 startups spanning pre-seed to pre-Series A stages, with a preference for leading pre-seed and seed rounds. Vidyakul secures Rs 10 Cr debt funding from Michael & Susan Dell Foundation

Vernacular learning platform Vidyakul has secured Rs 10 crore in debt funding from the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation to expand its educational services across India. Indian nuclear technology startup SUK-M has raised its first institutional pre-seed funding round, led by Speciale Invest, with participation from Navam Capital, BYT Capital and two angel investors.
